divisions.question: Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 - Third Reading - Pass the bill
Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 - Second Reading - Agree with the bill's main idea
Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Introduced the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 bill to let a referendum ask Australians to add words to section 96 allowing the Commonwealth to grant financial assistance directly to local government, noting the Constitution has been amended only eight times in 112 years and similar proposals were rejected at referendums in 1974 and 1988.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Announced support for the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 from the government, opposition and minor parties, citing resolutions from over 490 councils and arguing that recognition would reflect Australia's three tiers of government without changing state accountability.

speeches.speaker: Ian Macfarlane
speeches.brief: Outlined the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 bill amending section 96 to let the Commonwealth make direct financial grants to local governments, following High Court rulings in the Pape and Williams cases that cast doubt on existing spending powers, noted direct payments total about $500 million a year including almost $2 billion in stimulus funding to more than 6,000 projects over five years, and cited a poll finding 61 per cent public support despite opposition from the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales governments.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: Strongly supported the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, arguing the Pape and Williams High Court decisions created uncertainty over direct Commonwealth funding to local councils, and pointed to $7 million delivered to Blacktown City Council under the Roads to Recovery program as an example of funding now at risk.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, noting Australian Bureau of Statistics data showing the Commonwealth collects about 80 per cent of all government tax revenue while local councils get only about four per cent, despite delivering most services directly to communities.

speeches.speaker: Julie Owens
speeches.brief: Supported the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, explaining the amendment simply adds 17 words to section 96 of the Constitution to let the Commonwealth fund local councils directly, and cited $2.3 million delivered for local black spot funding in her Parramatta electorate since 2007.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: Supported the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum as a minimal fix addressing High Court uncertainty from the Pape and Williams cases, while criticising the government for giving only four months notice when the Electoral Commission said six months was needed, and praised the Roads to Recovery program as vital to his Parkes electorate's councils.

speeches.speaker: Geoff Lyons
speeches.brief: Supported the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, citing the Commonwealth's partnership with local government to deliver more than 6,000 community projects in five years, and noted recognition of local government was previously and unsuccessfully put to referendum by the Whitlam government in 1974 and the Hawke government in 1988.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Opposed the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, citing constitutional law professor Anne Twomey's view that the Pape and Williams cases did not actually threaten Commonwealth funding to councils, and warned the changes could let Canberra impose conditions on local grants, reducing council autonomy over community priorities.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Supported the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, arguing councils such as Shellharbour City Council face a vertical fiscal imbalance between service responsibilities and revenue-raising capacity, and noted that nearly 30 per cent of Australia's first federal parliamentarians elected in 1901 had served in local government.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: Opposed the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, noting previous attempts failed in 1974 under the Whitlam government and 1988 under the Hawke government, and criticised the government for allocating $21.6 million in public funding to the 'yes' case while giving nothing to the 'no' case.

speeches.speaker: Dennis Jensen
speeches.brief: Opposed the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) referendum, citing Senator Kate Lundy's admission in a Senate committee that the Williams case was not a justification for the change, and noted the Commonwealth already provides about $2.7 billion annually to local government, with around 20 per cent as direct funding.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Supported the local government referendum, saying the Commonwealth has partnered with local government to deliver over 6,000 community projects in the last five years, and cited the Ironsley River bridge in Far North Queensland, built for about $17 million in federal funding after the Queensland government had costed it at $31 million.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Summed up the local government referendum debate, saying the government has committed $10 million to a neutral civics education campaign rather than the $21.6 million claimed by the member for Mitchell, and rejected the member for Tangney's description of the bill as un-Australian, noting local government remains free to reject any Commonwealth assistance offered.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Back
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against the Constitution Alteration (Local Government) 2013 Bill, claiming it would concentrate power in Canberra at the expense of state governments and local councils. They criticised the government’s decision to allocate $10 million to the ‘yes’ campaign and only $500,000 to the ‘no’ campaign, and noted that several states oppose the amendment.

speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government’s proposed constitutional amendment on local government is likely to fail due to inadequate state support, a rushed timeline, and skewed public funding ($10 million for the Yes case versus $500,000 for the No case). He also accused Labor of using the referendum as a political distraction and noted that the Australian Electoral Commission had warned of insufficient preparation time.
